summary: Berkshire Hathaway’s 2024 Form 10-K cover identifies the company, Delaware incorporation, Omaha headquarters, fiscal year, listed common stock and senior notes, filing status, filer classification, internal-control attestation, market value, shares outstanding, and proxy material incorporated by reference. Its contents outline Parts I–IV: business, risks, cybersecurity, properties and legal matters; equity and market information, management analysis, market risks, financial statements and disclosures; governance, compensation, ownership and auditor matters; and exhibits, schedules, and signatures.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business Description
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway is a Delaware holding company headquartered in Omaha, with diverse subsidiaries led by insurance, rail transportation, and utility and energy businesses, as well as manufacturing, services, and retail. Its operating companies are managed with unusual decentralization; senior leaders oversee major capital allocation, investments, and operating CEO selection. Corporate management monitors governance, the board selects the CEO’s successor, and the ethics code sets standards for legal and ethical conduct. At year-end 2024, Berkshire employed about 392,400 people worldwide (80% in the U.S.; 20% union-represented). Subsidiaries set varied personnel policies covering safety, compensation and benefits, wellness, training and advancement, and recruitment. U.S. workforce data is available on Berkshire’s website.

nodes.title: Insurance Businesses
Insurance Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s global insurance subsidiaries insure and reinsure property, casualty, life, health and other risks, employing about 41,500 people. The text explains industry competition and U.S. and international regulation, including admitted and non-admitted insurance, NAIC and IAIS standards, group supervision, capital reporting, Berkshire’s Nebraska lead supervisor, and its strong capital and ratings. It outlines TRIA terrorism coverage, eligibility, deductibles, reimbursement and limits. It describes Berkshire’s underwriting groups and profit expectations, then details GEICO’s products, sales, competition, market share, regulation and claims operations, and BH Primary’s independently managed insurers, coverage, and 2024 premium mix. Alleghany’s acquisition and integration into the primary and reinsurance groups are also noted.

nodes.title: GEICO
nodes.summary: The text outlines the varied U.S. and international regulatory requirements and oversight affecting Berkshire’s insurance operations, including licensing, capital, solvency, governance, reporting, privacy, and cross-border legal obligations. It describes Berkshire’s underwriting groups, Alleghany’s acquisition and integration, underwriting-profit expectations, and detailed businesses, products, distribution, markets, competition, and locations of GEICO and BH Primary insurers. It explains BHRG’s global structure and treaty/facultative and proportional/excess reinsurance, market-dependent underwriting, property-casualty and life-health operations, and retroactive reinsurance, whose long-tail claims generally create underwriting losses but generate investment float.

nodes.title: Reinsurance Businesses and Market Conditions
nodes.summary: Business volumes vary with market conditions, pricing adequacy, coverage terms and large transactions. Property/casualty operations describe NICO, General Re and TransRe offerings, contract types, markets, distribution channels and IAG’s quota-share agreement through 2029. General Re also writes global life and health reinsurance, while BHLN covers traditional life and certain closed-block variable-annuity risks in run-off. Retroactive reinsurance covers claims from past events, often including long-tail exposures; expected losses typically exceed premiums, but investment income on generated funds supports the business.

nodes.title: Periodic payment annuity
nodes.summary: BHLN issues and reinsures long-term structured-settlement annuities, receiving upfront premiums while making future payments that generally exceed premiums; it wrote no new policies in 2023–24. Berkshire’s insurance investments are CEO-managed, concentrated in public equities alongside short-term and fixed-maturity securities, with no target allocations or liability-duration matching. Float, its components, growth from about $129 billion in 2019 to $171 billion in 2024, and its underwriting-based cost measure are described. BNSF’s operations, workforce, service regions, freight categories and pricing, network and partnerships, economic and competitive influences, and federal, state, and Canadian regulatory oversight—including rate, route, safety, health, environmental, and hazardous-material rules—are outlined.

Covers Berkshire’s insurance and reinsurance businesses, their products, markets, underwriting groups, competition, distribution, regulation, capital and ratings, including TRIA coverage and Alleghany’s integration. Details GEICO, BH Primary, BHRG’s property-casualty and life-health operations, treaty and facultative reinsurance, retroactive reinsurance, and structured-settlement annuities. It also describes insurance investments and float, including its growth and cost, and BNSF’s operations, network, freight, workforce, markets, partnerships, economic influences and regulatory oversight.

nodes.title: Burlington Northern Santa Fe
nodes.summary: BHLN’s structured-settlement annuities exchange upfront premiums for long-term payments, typically producing underwriting losses; it issued none in 2023–24. Berkshire’s insurance investments are CEO-managed, equity-heavy and concentrated, funded by capital and float, which grew from about $129 billion in 2019 to $171 billion in 2024. BNSF’s railroad operations, workforce, freight markets, routes, revenues, regulation, environmental liabilities and emissions-reduction plans are described, along with competition from rail and other transport. BHE’s energy and real-estate businesses, customers, pipelines, workforce and utilities are outlined, including PacifiCorp’s service territory, economic diversity and wholesale power trading.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy
Energy businesses
nodes.summary: BNSF faces extensive environmental regulation, cleanup and third-party liability risks, and locomotive diesel produced about 80% of its 2018 GHG emissions; it targets a 30% reduction by 2030 through efficiency, renewable diesel and evaluation of battery-electric and hydrogen locomotives. Rail competition comes from other railroads and transport modes, especially trucks, and drives efficiency improvements; Union Pacific is its main Western competitor. Berkshire Hathaway Energy (BHE) is a diversified energy holding company with U.S. regulated utilities serving 5.3 million customers, extensive gas pipelines, international electricity networks, renewable power projects, LNG facilities, real-estate interests and about 24,000 employees. Its utilities serve varied regional economies, own about 31,300 MW of generation, buy and sell energy, and face seasonal demand. The text describes PacifiCorp, MidAmerican and Nevada utilities; BHE GT&S, Northern Natural and Kern River pipeline and storage operations; UK and Canadian electricity networks; independent generation projects totaling about 6,100 MW, mainly renewable and under long-term contracts; and $7.3 billion in third-party wind tax-equity investments.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: U.S. utilities face extensive federal, state and local oversight. FERC regulates wholesale electricity rates, transmission, reliability, utility holding companies, records, securities, hydro facilities and related matters, and may impose substantial daily penalties; MEC is also subject to NRC oversight of its Quad Cities Nuclear Station ownership. Utilities generally have exclusive retail service territories and service obligations, though customer choice and self-generation are permitted in some jurisdictions. State commissions typically set cost-of-service retail rates allowing reasonable cost recovery and returns, with bundled and transmission- or distribution-only options. UK Northern Powergrid distribution fees are formula-controlled for 2023–2028. Alberta’s AUC regulates AltaLink’s tariffs, rates, construction, operations and financing, while AESO operates and plans the integrated system and wholesale market. Natural gas pipelines and storage are federally and state regulated: FERC oversees named companies’ rates, service, facilities and LNG operations, and DOT’s pipeline safety office enforces federal safety requirements.

nodes.title: Environmental Matters
nodes.summary: BHE faces extensive environmental laws, compliance costs, penalties, and potential effects on operations, including air-quality rules and clean-energy standards. The text outlines the Paris Agreement’s goals and U.S. commitments, withdrawal and reentry, updated targets, and growing state and local clean-energy demands. It describes EPA power-sector greenhouse-gas standards and oil-and-gas methane rules, their requirements, litigation, and possible reevaluation. BHE’s emissions primarily come from coal and gas generation; it reports renewable and storage investments, coal-unit closures, a 38% emissions reduction since 2005, and plans for further reductions and investment toward a 50% cut by 2030, subject to customer, reliability, cost, and regulatory considerations.

nodes.title: Non-Energy Businesses
nodes.summary: HomeServices of America is a U.S. residential real estate brokerage offering traditional brokerage and integrated services such as mortgage, title, insurance, warranties, relocation and other home-related services. It operates 48 brands across 34 states and Washington, D.C., with about 37,700 agents in nearly 820 offices. Its franchise network has about 270 franchisees, over 1,400 offices and 44,700 third-party agents using two brands; services include brand rights, training, consultation and advertising in exchange for fees. Revenue depends on transaction volume, typically higher in the second and third quarters, and the business faces strong competition and general real estate market conditions.

Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s diversified operations include regulated U.S. utilities, gas pipelines and storage, international electricity networks, contracted generation and renewable-energy investments, alongside real-estate businesses. The section covers energy operations and competition; extensive federal, state, local, UK and Canadian regulation of utilities, markets, pipelines and safety; and environmental laws, emissions, litigation, compliance costs and emissions-reduction plans. It also describes HomeServices of America’s brokerage and related services, franchise network, seasonality and exposure to competition and housing-market conditions.

nodes.title: Manufacturing Businesses
Industrial products
nodes.summary: Berkshire groups its manufacturing subsidiaries into industrial, building, and consumer products, employing about 180,000 people at year-end 2024. The groups cover industrial components and chemicals; homes, construction materials, and related products; and recreational vehicles, batteries, apparel, footwear, and other goods. The text details Precision Castparts (PCC), based in Oregon, which makes complex metal components, castings, forgings, alloys, fasteners, aerostructures, and composites for aerospace, power and energy, and other markets. It describes PCC’s casting and forging technologies and applications, its diverse end markets, major customers including Boeing, Airbus, GE Aerospace, Rolls-Royce, and Pratt & Whitney, and sales largely governed by long-term agreements, with few cancellations but occasional delivery delays.

nodes.title: Precision Castparts
nodes.summary: HomeServices of America provides residential brokerage and integrated home services through owned offices and a large franchise network; revenue depends on seasonal housing transactions and market conditions. Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses span industrial, building and consumer products and employed about 180,000 people in 2024. Precision Castparts makes specialized metal components, alloys, castings, forgings, fasteners and aerospace structures; its prospects depend on aerospace demand and production capacity, amid competition, concentrated raw-material sourcing and evolving environmental obligations. Lubrizol produces specialty additives and advanced materials for global transportation, industrial and consumer markets, relying on technology, intellectual property, worldwide operations and supply relationships while managing competition, disruptions, safety, cybersecurity, reliability and environmental compliance.

nodes.title: Lubrizol
nodes.summary: PCC faces expected aerospace growth but depends on scaling production and resolving OEM supply constraints; it competes through customer ties, expertise, facilities and workforce, while relying on scarce, geopolitically and economically sensitive alloy metals and facing evolving environmental rules and potentially significant costs. Lubrizol’s two specialty-chemicals segments, products, competitors, innovation and IP, global operations and customers, raw-material sourcing, supply disruptions, safety, cybersecurity, environmental investments and regulatory risks are described. IMC’s carbide cutting-tool brands, products, manufacturing and sales networks, customers, competitors, tungsten supply exposure and environmental commitments are outlined. Marmon’s global, diverse operations and its Foodservice Technologies, Water Technologies and Transportation Products groups, offerings and geographic reach are introduced.

nodes.title: IMC International Metalworking Companies
nodes.summary: Lubrizol faces environmental, safety, trade and other regulatory requirements; despite risk controls, chemical manufacturing carries inherent risks and potential future costs or liabilities. IMC is a leading global maker of precision carbide cutting tools, detailing its brands, products, manufacturing and distribution footprint, customers, engineering, competition, tungsten supply risks, and environmental compliance. Marmon is a Chicago-based global organization with 11 business groups and over 120 businesses across roughly 650 facilities; its Foodservice Technologies, Water Technologies and Transportation Products groups serve diverse markets with equipment, treatment systems, components and related products across multiple countries.

nodes.title: Marmon
nodes.summary: Lubrizol faces environmental, safety, product and trade regulation, with chemical manufacturing carrying inherent risks and potential future costs or liabilities. IMC is a global carbide cutting-tool manufacturer, detailing its brands, products, facilities, engineering, customers, distribution, competitors, tungsten supply exposure and environmental compliance. Marmon is a diversified global organization with eleven business groups spanning foodservice, water, transportation, retail, metals, electrical, plumbing and HVAC-R, industrial products, rail and leasing, crane services and medical devices. The text describes each group’s offerings and geographic reach, including UTLX railcars and EXSIF tank containers, their leasing and market characteristics, and notes regulatory oversight and ongoing environmental monitoring and remediation.

nodes.title: Other industrial products
nodes.summary: The industrial products group includes CTB, a global agricultural systems manufacturer serving grain preservation, livestock and food production and processing through worldwide facilities and distributors. It competes on price, value, reputation, quality, design and service, supported by strong brands, broad products and distribution; its main materials have been adequately available. LSPI is a global pipeline drag-reduction technology and service provider, treating over 50 million barrels of hydrocarbon liquids daily across 24 countries and five continents, and is subject to environmental and emissions laws. W&W|AFCO is a North American structural steel fabricator and construction business with 19 U.S. plants, a substantial multiyear 2024 project backlog, and projects across industrial, commercial, infrastructure and military sectors. Acquired in October 2022 with Alleghany, it is headquartered in Oklahoma City.

nodes.title: Building Products
nodes.summary: Clayton is a Knoxville-area vertically integrated housing company offering factory-built and site-built homes, financing and related services. In 2024 it completed about 51,000 off-site homes (over 95% meeting DOE Zero Energy Ready Home requirements) and 10,000 site-built homes; its off-site backlog was about $700 million. It sells through multiple channels and uses proprietary underwriting for retail financing. Its site-built division has nine builders, nearly 300 subdivisions across 18 states, about 66,000 controlled homesites and a $1.46 billion backlog. Input supplies were adequate in 2023–24, though historically volatile. Mortgage-rate increases in 2022–23 slowed demand, partly offset by low existing-home inventory; rates eased slightly late in 2024. Operations incur environmental-compliance costs, while lending is subject to federal and state regulation and government oversight.

nodes.title: Clayton
nodes.summary: The text outlines Berkshire businesses across industrial and building products. CTB’s competitors, competitive strengths, materials and supply availability are described; LSPI’s global pipeline drag-reduction solutions and environmental regulation are summarized; and W&W|AFCO’s steel operations, projects, backlog and acquisition history are noted. Clayton’s home offerings, production, channels, financing, backlogs, inputs, interest-rate sensitivity and regulatory obligations are covered. Shaw’s flooring, turf and environmental products, sales and distribution, materials, competition and pricing factors are detailed. Johns Manville’s products, facilities, patents, raw materials and extensive environmental compliance responsibilities are also described.

nodes.title: Shaw
nodes.summary: Shaw, based in Dalton, Georgia, manufactures and distributes carpet, carpet tile and diverse hard-surface flooring, with integrated carpet production, international operations, installation/project services, synthetic turf businesses and Watershed environmental and renewable-energy solutions. It sells globally through a large wholesale network and distribution system. Carpet uses mostly nylon, polypropylene, polyester and recycled inputs; Shaw processes most yarn internally, while raw-material costs reflect energy prices and may be passed on. Flooring competition centers on quality, style, price and service; carpet represented about 44% of U.S. flooring consumption in 2023. Johns Manville, headquartered in Denver, makes insulation, roofing, fiberglass reinforcement and technical nonwovens for many markets, operating 40-plus North American and European facilities and research centers. It uses fiberglass, other chemicals and recycled materials; supplies are generally adequate, though recycled-glass availability varies. Patents are valuable but no business depends materially on one. JM monitors extensive U.S., Canadian and European environmental regulations, and compliance is incorporated into capital projects.

nodes.title: Johns Manville
nodes.summary: The text profiles five building-products businesses. Shaw makes and distributes residential and commercial flooring, turf, and environmental and renewable-energy solutions; it describes its products, global channels, integrated and recycled-material manufacturing, raw-material costs, distribution network, and competitive conditions. Johns Manville makes insulation, roofing, fiberglass, and technical materials, outlining markets, facilities, R&D, patents, raw materials, environmental regulation, sales channels, competition, and seasonality. MiTek supplies building hardware, engineered components, software, and machinery worldwide, noting customers and steel supply risks. Benjamin Moore produces and sells premium coatings through retailers and online, covering brands, competition, ingredients, and environmental matters. Acme manufactures brick and block and distributes other building products, describing markets, facilities, seasonality, construction cycles, and adequate raw-material supplies.

nodes.title: JM, MiTek, Benjamin Moore and Acme Businesses
nodes.summary: The page outlines JM’s sales channels, competitive positioning, product advantages and seasonal demand. MiTek’s global operations, residential and commercial markets, customers and galvanized-steel supply risks are described. Benjamin Moore’s coating brands, retail and online distribution, Ace relationship, competition, raw materials, and environmental compliance and remediation are covered. Acme’s brick, block and distributed products, markets and customers, manufacturing sites, seasonal and cyclical demand, and adequate raw-material resources are also summarized.

nodes.title: Acme
nodes.summary: The text outlines JM’s sales channels, competition, market position, product differentiators and seasonal demand; MiTek’s global residential and commercial building operations, products, customers and galvanized-steel supply risks; and Benjamin Moore’s coating brands, retail and online distribution, competition, raw materials and environmental compliance and remediation. It describes Acme’s brick and block products, facilities, markets, seasonal and cyclical demand, raw-material supply and MACT compliance. Consumer businesses covered include Forest River’s vehicles, dealers, market share, competition and safety regulation; Fruit of the Loom’s apparel brands, production, sourcing, raw materials and competition; Garan’s children’s clothing operations; and Fechheimer’s public-service and safety uniforms.

nodes.title: Brick Regulations and Consumer Products
nodes.summary: Acme’s brick plants comply with EPA MACT standards under the Clean Air Act, which limit certain hazardous air pollutants and acidic gases. Forest River, headquartered in Indiana, manufactures RVs, cargo trailers, buses, and pontoon boats across seven states, selling varied brands in the U.S. and Canada through independent dealers. The competitive RV industry is concentrated; as of September 2024, the largest company held about 40% market share and Forest River about 35%. Forest River is subject to U.S. and Canadian safety regulations, participates in an RV safety standards association, and believes its products materially comply.

nodes.title: Apparel and footwear
nodes.summary: The text surveys Berkshire’s apparel and footwear businesses: Fruit of the Loom’s product brands, markets, manufacturing locations, raw materials, supplier changes following 2021–22 disruptions, and competition; Garan’s children’s apparel, brands, operations, and U.S. distribution; Fechheimer’s public-service and safety uniforms; and BH Shoe Holdings’ work, outdoor, casual, and western footwear and Brooks’ performance running products. It also notes overseas sourcing, worldwide sales channels, and company-owned retail stores.

nodes.title: Other consumer products
nodes.summary: The consumer products group includes Duracell, a global battery manufacturer with production in the U.S., Europe and China, worldwide distribution, an estimated 32% share of the 2024 global alkaline battery market, and sufficient raw-material supply; Jazwares, acquired in 2022, which sells toys, games, costumes and pet products under owned and licensed brands in over 100 countries; Richline Group, whose four units make and distribute jewelry and other metal, gem and precious-metal products to retail, artisan and industrial customers; and Albecca, which operates across the U.S., Canada and 11 other countries, selling branded custom framing products and offering art printing and fulfillment.

Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses employ about 180,000 people and span industrial, building and consumer products. The section profiles industrial companies including Precision Castparts, Lubrizol, IMC, Marmon, CTB, LSPI and W&W|AFCO, covering their products, markets, operations, competition, supply chains, growth prospects and environmental and regulatory risks. Building businesses include Clayton, Shaw, Johns Manville, MiTek, Benjamin Moore and Acme, with discussion of homes, flooring, materials, financing, sales, demand cycles, inputs and compliance. Consumer businesses include Forest River, apparel and footwear makers, Duracell, Jazwares, Richline and Albecca, covering products, brands, production, sourcing, distribution, market positions and safety regulation.

nodes.title: Pilot Travel Centers
nodes.summary: Berkshire acquired full ownership and control of Pilot between 2017 and 2024. Pilot operates U.S. and Canadian travel centers, fuel retail, wholesale and marketing businesses, oil-field water disposal, and EV charging; the text details its locations, fuel volumes, workforce, services, competition, customer and supplier concentration, and environmental obligations. McLane’s three wholesale distribution units serve retail, restaurant, and beverage customers nationwide, with major customers, facilities, reach, and workforce described. Berkshire’s service businesses and employment are outlined, followed by FlightSafety’s aviation training, simulator manufacturing, regulatory compliance, and R&D, and NetJets’ global private aviation and shared-aircraft ownership offerings.

nodes.title: McLane
nodes.summary: Pilot is subject to environmental laws governing pollution, hazardous-waste-site remediation, and penalties for noncompliance; retirement of long-lived assets such as petroleum tanks, dispensers, and disposal wells may create asset retirement obligations. McLane provides wholesale distribution across all 50 states to retail, restaurant, and other customers; its 2024 major customers were Walmart (17.3% of revenue), 7-Eleven (13.2%), and Yum! Brands (12.5%). Its high-volume, rapid-turnover, cost-controlled business has three units: retail distribution serves about 46,400 locations through 26 facilities in 20 states; restaurant distribution serves about 32,000 restaurants through 45 facilities in 22 states; and beverage distribution, operated as Empire Distributors, serves about 30,200 locations in four states. McLane employed approximately 24,800 people at year-end 2024.

nodes.title: Service and Retailing Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s service businesses employ about 30,400 people and span aviation training and simulators (FlightSafety), private aviation and aircraft programs (NetJets), electronic-component distribution (TTI), trailer leasing (XTRA), restaurant franchising (Dairy Queen), news distribution (Business Wire), furniture rental (CORT), television and media (WPLG), logistics (Charter Brokerage), and regulated design, engineering, construction and consulting services (IPS). Its retailing businesses employ about 26,000 people and include automotive dealerships and related services (BHA), regional home-furnishings retailers, jewelry chains, See’s confectionery, Pampered Chef kitchenware, Oriental Trading online products, and Louis motorcycle apparel and equipment. The text outlines their offerings, locations, scale, customers, operations, competition, regulations, and seasonality.

nodes.title: Additional information with respect to Berkshire’s businesses
nodes.summary: The text directs readers to financial statement notes for segment revenue, pretax earnings, assets, and fixed-maturity and equity investments. It reports Berkshire’s approximately 27% stake in Kraft Heinz and 28% stake in Occidental as of year-end 2024, describes both companies’ businesses, and points to Note 5 for investment details. It also explains how to access Berkshire’s corporate materials and SEC filings online or request free copies by mail.

nodes.title: Berkshire Risk Factors
key_items: General Business Risks Terrorist acts could hurt our operating businesses.
Cybersecurity risks could result in economic losses to our businesses and reputational damage.
Geopolitical events could cause losses to our business and losses in the values of securities we own.
We are dependent on a few key people for our major investment and capital allocation decisions.
nodes.summary: Berkshire warns that its listed risks are not exhaustive and unknown or currently immaterial risks may emerge. Terrorist attacks could cause casualties, property and operational losses. Cyberattacks may disrupt systems and operations, expose information, harm reputation, increase costs, impair financial results or access to capital, and hinder competitiveness despite mitigation planning. Geopolitical conflicts and trade restrictions could disrupt businesses and reduce security values. Major investment and capital decisions depend on a few executives, especially Warren Buffett; a board succession plan and experienced operating managers partly mitigate this risk.

nodes.title: Key Business and Financial Risks
key_items: We need qualified personnel to manage and operate our various businesses.
Investments are unusually concentrated in equity securities and fair values are subject to loss in value.
Competition and technology may erode our business franchises and result in lower earnings.
Unfavorable general economic conditions may significantly reduce our operating earnings and impair our ability to access capital markets at a reasonable cost.
Epidemics, pandemics or other similar outbreaks could hurt our operating businesses.
Regulatory changes may adversely impact our future operating results.
nodes.summary: The page outlines risks from difficulties recruiting and retaining qualified personnel and labor disruptions; concentrated equity investments losing value and weakening earnings, shareholders’ equity, insurance surplus, ratings, and underwriting capacity; competition and technological change eroding business advantages; economic downturns, inflation, or costly or restricted capital-market access; epidemics disrupting operations, supply chains, demand, customers’ creditworthiness, and investment values; and regulatory changes that raise compliance costs or create financial, reputational, and penalty risks, including data-privacy rules.

nodes.title: Climate and Insurance Underwriting Risks
key_items: Climate change and the regulation of greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions may impact our businesses.
Risks unique to our regulated businesses Our tolerance for underwriting risk assumed in our various insurance businesses may result in significant underwriting losses.
nodes.summary: Climate change and extreme weather may damage operations and assets, increase insurance losses, and raise compliance costs as GHG policies evolve; regulatory noncompliance could harm financial results. The insurers’ willingness to assume substantial catastrophe risk, despite underwriting safeguards and policy limits, can lead to unexpected losses and lower earnings. Claims liabilities are difficult to estimate and may grow as legal, social, environmental, and industry conditions change, expanding coverage and litigation exposure. Uncertainty over long-tail claims and even small increases in the $147.6 billion of estimated unpaid property-and-casualty losses could materially reduce earnings.

nodes.title: Changes in regulations and regulatory actions can adversely affect our operating results and our ability to allocate capital.
nodes.summary: Regulatory changes and enforcement may constrain Berkshire’s insurance businesses’ operations, investments, capital, and dividends, harming results and capital allocation. BNSF faces extensive railroad regulation, compliance costs, litigation, and possible legislative changes; restrictions on coal use could reduce revenue, hazardous-material releases could create major liabilities, and rail rules may limit pricing and investment. BHE utilities and energy operations face complex, changing regulation affecting assets, rates, financing, transactions, and dividends, along with environmental, wildfire, and cost-recovery risks. Railroad and utility systems require substantial long-term capital investment, whose failures may not be recoverable through rates; reliance on debt makes access to disrupted capital markets a further risk to results, liquidity, and resources.

nodes.title: Item 1C. Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s cybersecurity framework lets business groups tailor risk controls while supporting consistent reporting. CISOs report annually to group management and internal audit; groups must report significant incidents and monitor third-party risks, which may cause major financial, operational, or reputational harm. The Audit Committee oversees the program, incidents, trends, and IT/cyber audits; business-group management handles daily protection, and Berkshire management considers SEC reporting. The properties section describes BNSF’s rail network across 28 states and three Canadian provinces, its owned and trackage-rights miles, operational facilities, equipment and transfer hubs, and $2.4 billion in 2024 repairs and maintenance expense.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity Oversight and BNSF Properties
nodes.summary: Berkshire and its business groups monitor cybersecurity risks from third-party providers. The Board Audit Committee oversees the cybersecurity program through incident and trend reports and approval of internal audits, including testing and assessments; business-group management handles daily protection, reports significant events, and Berkshire management considers SEC reporting. The properties section notes the substantial physical assets used by railroad and utilities businesses. BNSF operates more than 32,500 route miles across 28 states and three Canadian provinces, including owned track and trackage rights, and more than 50,000 total track miles. Its facilities, equipment, network systems, and transfer hubs support rail operations; it owns or leases about 6,800 locomotives and 71,400 freight cars and recorded $2.4 billion in 2024 repairs and maintenance.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy
nodes.summary: BHE’s energy properties support its electricity and natural gas businesses, include generation, mining, transmission, distribution, pipeline, storage, LNG and related rights, and are largely pledged against subsidiary debt. The text lists operating generation sources, entities, locations and facility/net-owned capacities at year-end 2024, defines those capacity measures, and reports 1,085 MW of generation under construction plus battery storage of 320 MW operating and 527 MW under construction. It also summarizes the miles and facilities of utility transmission/distribution systems and the pipeline, storage and LNG operations of BHE GT&S, Northern Natural and Kern River, plus Northern Powergrid and AltaLink electricity networks.

nodes.title: Other Segments
nodes.summary: The text summarizes physical-property data for Berkshire’s other business segments: insurance, manufacturing, Pilot, McLane, service, and retailing. It lists operating countries or locations, property and facility types, and the numbers owned and leased, covering offices, claims centers, factories, warehouses, retail sites, travel and fuel facilities, terminals, housing subdivisions, training facilities, and other specialized properties.

nodes.title: Legal Matters, Mine Safety, and Executive Officers
nodes.summary: Berkshire and subsidiaries face routine insurance, reinsurance, and other legal actions, including some seeking punitive damages or fines; the company does not expect pending matters to materially affect its financial condition or results, with certain litigation detailed in Note 27. Mine safety disclosures appear in Exhibit 95. The page lists four executive officers, their ages, positions, and service start years, and explains their terms continue until successors qualify or their service otherwise ends.

summary: Part I describes Berkshire Hathaway’s structure, decentralized management, governance, workforce, and diverse insurance, railroad, energy, manufacturing, travel, wholesale, service, and retail businesses, including their operations, markets, properties, competition, regulation, and environmental obligations. It covers investments and major equity holdings; business, financial, climate, underwriting, regulatory, personnel, and cybersecurity risks and oversight; unresolved comments (none); legal matters, mine-safety disclosures, and executive officers; and directs readers to financial statement notes, corporate materials, and SEC filings.

nodes.title: Shareholders, Dividends, Repurchases and Stock Performance
key_items: Shareholders; Dividends; Stock Performance Graph; Item 6. [Reserved]
nodes.summary: Reports Berkshire’s February 2025 Class A and B record holders and nominee-held shares, notes no cash dividends since 1967, and describes its repurchase program: Buffett may authorize purchases below conservatively estimated intrinsic value, but none occurred in Q4 2024. The program has no set share or dollar limit or expiration date, subject to a $30 billion cash, equivalents and Treasury-bills floor. A graph compares a $100 investment from 2019 with two S&P indices, with notes on dividend reinvestment and the insurance index rationale. Item 6 is reserved.

nodes.title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations Results of Operations
nodes.summary: The section reports Berkshire’s after-tax earnings by business segment for 2022–2024, excluding noncontrolling interests, and notes that segment data should be read with the financial-statement disclosures. It cautions that macroeconomic, geopolitical, industry and company-specific factors make future effects unpredictable. It explains year-to-year results: insurance underwriting improved with GEICO, despite catastrophe and settlement costs; insurance investment income rose on higher short-term investment yields; BNSF declined amid freight, cost, labor and litigation factors; utilities and energy rose in 2024 after wildfire accruals fell, following a 2023 decline; and manufacturing, service and retailing declined slightly in 2024 after growing in 2023, with results reflecting varied business performance and acquisitions.

It discusses underwriting volatility from catastrophes, prior-loss estimates and currency changes; insurance operations and long-tail retroactive reinsurance/annuity economics; significant catastrophe losses, including an estimated $1.3 billion from January 2025 California wildfires; and underwriting results by group for 2022–24. GEICO’s business model and results are detailed: 2024 earnings improved on higher premiums, fewer claims and efficiency, partly offset by severity, catastrophe losses and adverse prior-year development; 2023 improved over 2022 through rate increases, lower frequency, favorable development and lower expenses, despite rising severities. Premium, loss, expense, ratio, frequency, severity, policy-count and prior-year reserve-development trends are reported for both comparisons.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group comprises independently managed insurers providing commercial coverage across healthcare professional liability, workers’ compensation, auto, general liability, property and specialty lines for businesses of all sizes. Its insurers include BHSI, RSUI, CapSpecialty, BHHC, MedPro, GUARD, NICO Primary, BH Direct and USLI. The text presents 2022–2024 underwriting results. In 2024, premiums written rose 3.8% to $18.836 billion, mainly from NICO Primary, BH Direct and BHHC growth, partly offset by GUARD’s 16.3% decline after it exited admitted homeowners and tightened underwriting. Losses and loss-adjustment expenses rose 12.8%, and the loss ratio increased 2.1 percentage points. Prior-year loss estimates were reduced by $52 million in 2024 versus $537 million in 2023; the change reflected GUARD’s higher claim estimates, less favorable development elsewhere amid social inflation, partly offset by greater property-loss estimate reductions. GUARD’s review followed deteriorating claims experience, and catastrophe losses were about $350 million in 2024 versus minimal in 2023.

nodes.title: Berkshire Insurance Underwriting Results
nodes.summary: The page reports Primary Group underwriting trends: 2024 expenses rose $681 million and the expense ratio increased to 27.8%, mainly due to business mix and GUARD costs; in 2023, premiums written, losses and expenses rose, reflecting acquisitions and business mix, while catastrophe losses declined and prior-year liability estimates were reduced. It describes Reinsurance Group coverage and subsidiaries, lists pre-tax results by business line and property/casualty underwriting figures for 2022–2024, and notes 2024 written premiums fell 2.1% while earned premiums increased 1.4%.

nodes.title: Property/casualty
nodes.summary: The discussion reviews underwriting results for Berkshire Hathaway Primary and Reinsurance Groups. Primary Group expenses rose 15% and its expense ratio increased in 2024, mainly due to business mix and GUARD costs; in 2023, premiums, losses and expenses grew, reflecting acquisitions, business mix and catastrophe-loss changes, while prior-year liabilities declined. The Reinsurance Group’s businesses and 2022–2024 property/casualty results are outlined. In 2024, written premiums fell slightly, earned premiums rose, losses and the loss ratio declined, and expenses increased, including a $490 million settlement charge and currency effects; prior-year liabilities were reduced. In 2023, premiums, losses and expenses rose substantially, largely following the TransRe acquisition, with catastrophe losses, reserve reductions and foreign-exchange effects also discussed.

nodes.title: Life/health
nodes.summary: The life/health reinsurance table reports 2022–2024 premiums written and earned, benefits, expenses, and pre-tax underwriting earnings. Premiums earned fell $74 million in 2024, including the comparison impact of $161 million in 2023 contract commutations; excluding this, they declined $235 million (4.5%), mainly due to non-U.S. life business, while 2023 was nearly unchanged from 2022. Underwriting earnings fell $131 million in 2024 after rising $245 million in 2023. Commutation gains were $53 million in 2024 and $134 million in 2023. Excluding gains, 2024 earnings declined $50 million, as weaker non-U.S. life results and greater U.S. long-term care run-off losses were partly offset by stronger U.S. life results.

nodes.title: Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: Retroactive reinsurance results reflect claim estimates, deferred charges and currency movements: losses before currency effects were $898 million in 2024, $1.5 billion in 2023 and $836 million in 2022, while currency effects varied from gains of $52 million and $168 million to a $57 million loss. Prior-year liabilities rose, especially in 2023 due to asbestos, environmental and casualty claims; unpaid losses and deferred charges declined in 2024. Periodic payment annuity wrote no new business in 2023–24 amid inadequate rates; results include liability accretion and currency effects, and liabilities totaled $14.3 billion at 2024 year-end. Variable annuity guarantee reinsurance, in run-off, earned $157 million, $233 million and $467 million in 2024, 2023 and 2022. Insurance investment income rose to $13.67 billion in 2024, driven chiefly by higher Treasury bill and short-term investment balances; the company prioritizes liquidity and safety over yield.

nodes.title: Insurance Underwriting and Annuity Results
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group’s prior-year claim estimates rose in 2022–2024, with the largest 2023 increase reflecting asbestos, environmental and casualty claims and a $650 million pretax loss; retroactive reinsurance unpaid losses and deferred charges declined in 2024, with charges recognized over settlement periods. Periodic payment annuity business is sensitive to prices, demand and claim settlements; no new business was written in 2023 or 2024 due to inadequate rates. Pretax losses reflected liability accretion and currency effects, with losses before currency effects of $596 million, $590 million and $694 million in 2024, 2023 and 2022; 2022 included a $130 million contract-termination loss. Year-end 2024 liabilities were $14.3 billion, including $4.0 billion without life contingencies, excluding discount-rate changes in OCI. Variable annuity guarantee reinsurance, in run-off, earned $157 million, $233 million and $467 million in 2024, 2023 and 2022; results depend on markets, interest rates and currency.

Reviews 2022–2024 insurance underwriting and investment results, including investment-gain and underwriting volatility from catastrophes, reserve estimates and currencies, and major catastrophe losses, notably the estimated $1.3 billion from January 2025 California wildfires. It covers GEICO’s business model and trends in premiums, claims, expenses, ratios, policies and reserve development; Primary Group businesses, results, growth, losses and expenses; and Reinsurance Group property/casualty and life/health results. It also examines retroactive reinsurance reserves, deferred charges and currency effects, periodic-payment annuity liabilities and losses, variable-annuity guarantee reinsurance in run-off, and investment income and liquidity priorities.

nodes.title: Insurance—Investment Income
nodes.summary: Insurance investment income is reported for 2022–2024. Net investment income rose from $6.484 billion in 2022 to $9.567 billion in 2023 and $13.670 billion in 2024, reflecting changes in interest and other investment income, dividends, taxes, and noncontrolling interests; effective tax rates were 16.0%, 17.4%, and 18.4%, respectively. Interest income increased $5.5 billion in 2024, mainly due to larger Treasury bill and short-term investment balances, and $4.4 billion in 2023, driven by greater short-term balances, higher rates, and acquired Alleghany insurance assets. The company prioritizes liquidity and safety over yield for short-term investments.

nodes.title: Insurance—Investment Income
Insurance—Investment Income (intro)
nodes.summary: Insurance investment income details declining dividend income in 2024 and 2023, driven by reduced equity holdings partly offset by higher dividend rates, and explains dividend variability. It defines insurance float, reports balances of $171 billion, $169 billion and $164 billion for 2024–2022, and notes negative average float costs in 2024–2023 and nominal cost in 2022. It lists insurance cash and investments for 2024–2023 and 2024 fixed-maturity holdings, values and credit ratings. The BNSF section describes its rail network and business groups, presents 2022–2024 earnings and freight volumes, and discusses 2024 revenue, earnings and operating-cost factors, plus consumer and industrial product results and volume drivers.

nodes.title: Burlington Northern Santa Fe
nodes.summary: The text reviews BNSF’s 2024 and 2023 results versus prior years, including earnings, freight volumes, revenues and expenses by business group, and the effects of pricing, fuel surcharges, customer demand, labor costs, productivity, litigation and natural gas prices. It also describes BHE’s businesses and regulated-rate framework, presents consolidated earnings and effective tax rates (including production tax credits), and compares after-tax earnings by utilities, pipelines, other energy, real estate brokerage, and corporate interest and other.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy
nodes.summary: BHE’s businesses, regulated-rate framework and 2022–2024 earnings are presented by segment. In 2024, U.S. utilities’ earnings rebounded as wildfire accruals fell and margins, tax credits and other income rose, partly offset by higher costs and interest; pipeline and other-energy earnings increased, while real-estate brokerage declined amid litigation and housing-market constraints. The text also explains 2023-versus-2022 segment trends, including wildfire-related utility losses and weaker other-energy and brokerage results. Manufacturing, service and retailing revenue, pre-tax earnings, net earnings, tax rates and margins are summarized for 2022–2024, with acquisition-accounting exclusions noted.

Covers insurance investment income, including declining dividends, insurance float balances and costs, cash and investments, and fixed-maturity holdings and credit ratings. Reviews BNSF’s network, business groups, 2022–2024 earnings, freight volumes, revenues and expenses, and factors such as pricing, demand, fuel, labor, productivity and litigation. Describes BHE’s businesses, regulated-rate framework, earnings, taxes and segment results, including wildfire effects, tax credits and market conditions. Summarizes manufacturing, service and retailing revenues, earnings, tax rates and margins, noting acquisition-accounting exclusions.

nodes.title: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s 2023 natural gas pipeline net earnings rose $39 million, driven by higher regulated service revenues and lower Cove Point noncontrolling-interest earnings, partly offset by increased expenses. Other energy earnings fell $332 million due to Northern Powergrid upstream business losses, U.K. Energy Profits Levy taxes, and weaker renewable results, partly offset by debt-extinguishment gains. Real estate brokerage earnings declined $87 million amid lower revenues and margins and reduced transaction volumes. The text then introduces a manufacturing, service, and retailing revenue and earnings table for 2022–2024 and year-over-year percentage changes.

Reviews 2022–2024 insurance underwriting, catastrophe and reserve volatility, GEICO, Primary and Reinsurance Group results, retroactive and annuity reinsurance liabilities, investment income, float, liquidity, cash and fixed-income holdings. It also covers BNSF’s network, earnings, volumes, revenues, costs and operating drivers; BHE’s regulated businesses, segment earnings, taxes, wildfire impacts, energy and market conditions; and manufacturing, service, retailing and real estate brokerage revenues, earnings, margins and trends, including acquisition-accounting exclusions.

nodes.title: Pre-tax earnings
nodes.summary: The text presents earnings data, including pre-tax earnings, taxes, net earnings, effective tax rates, and pre-tax margins for 2022–2024, noting that net earnings exclude specified after-tax acquisition-accounting expenses. It then summarizes manufacturing revenues and pre-tax earnings by industrial, building, and consumer products, with year-over-year changes and margins. Industrial products encompass PCC, Lubrizol, IMC, Marmon, and other businesses. In 2024, industrial revenue and earnings rose; PCC grew on aerospace and power demand and efficiency gains, while Lubrizol revenue was flat as higher volume offset lower prices and mix, and earnings increased due to lower costs and higher volumes.

Industrial products

nodes.title: Building products
nodes.summary: The text outlines Berkshire’s building products and consumer products businesses and their 2024-versus-2023 and 2023-versus-2022 results. Building products covers home construction and finance, flooring, insulation, roofing, masonry, coatings, and construction systems. In 2024, group revenue rose 2.2% while pretax earnings fell 1.3%. Clayton Homes revenue grew on higher home sales and financial-services income, with loan balances and affiliate funding increasing, but earnings declined due to insurance claims, loan-loss provisions, borrowing costs, and higher homebuilding costs. Other businesses had lower revenue but higher earnings from improved margins and efficiency, partly offset by expenses and weaker sales. In 2023, higher mortgage rates contributed to declines in group revenue and earnings; Clayton and other businesses faced lower sales, margins, and efficiencies, partly offset by financial-services growth and lower input costs. Consumer products includes leisure vehicles, apparel and footwear, batteries, toys, jewelry, and framing. In 2024, revenue and earnings increased, driven by Forest River, Brooks Sports, Duracell, apparel and footwear margins, and cost savings; some businesses declined, including Jazwares earnings. In 2023, revenue fell as Forest River and apparel sales weakened amid macroeconomic pressures, partly offset by Jazwares acquisition revenue; Duracell was roughly flat.

nodes.title: Consumer products
nodes.summary: Clayton Homes’ 2023 pretax earnings fell 13.8% to $2.0 billion as homebuilding sales and margins weakened, partly offset by stronger financial-services income. Other building products revenue and pretax earnings declined 10.0% and 11.4%, respectively, due to lower volumes, mix, efficiency and restructuring effects, partly offset by higher prices and lower costs. Consumer products includes vehicle, apparel, footwear, battery, toy, jewelry and framing businesses. In 2024, its revenue rose 2.2% and pretax earnings 10.9%, led by Forest River, Brooks Sports, Duracell and apparel/footwear improvements, despite weakness at some brands and Jazwares. In 2023, revenue fell 9.4%, mainly from Forest River and apparel/footwear declines, partly offset by Jazwares acquisition; pretax earnings rose 3.0%, as acquisition and apparel gains outweighed lower Forest River and Duracell earnings.

nodes.title: Service and retailing
nodes.summary: The text presents 2022–2024 revenues, pre-tax earnings, earnings margins, and year-over-year changes for Service, Retailing, Pilot, and McLane. It describes Service businesses, including aviation services, electronics distribution, restaurant franchising, equipment and furniture leasing, logistics, news and regulatory distribution, construction management, and a Miami television station; McLane is reported separately as a segment. Service revenue rose slightly to $20.7 billion in 2024 as aviation services and IPS growth offset declines at TTI and XTRA. Aviation revenue increased 9.1%, driven by more shared-ownership aircraft and flight hours; IPS revenue rose 14.4% on higher project volume.

Presents 2022–2024 revenues, pre-tax earnings, margins and year-over-year changes across industrial products, building products, consumer products, and service and retailing, including Pilot and McLane. Reviews the businesses in each group and explains performance drivers such as sales volumes, acquisitions, pricing, costs, margins, efficiency, financing, and economic or geopolitical conditions. Highlights company-level results, including growth and declines at PCC, Lubrizol, Marmon, IMC, Clayton Homes, Forest River, Brooks Sports, Duracell, Jazwares, and service businesses such as aviation and IPS.

nodes.title: Consumer Products Earnings and Service/Retailing Results
nodes.summary: Management discusses 2023 consumer products pre-tax earnings, up $46 million (3.0%) from 2022. Jazwares’ acquisition and stronger apparel and footwear earnings were partly offset by declines at Forest River, due mainly to lower sales volumes, and Duracell, due mainly to higher restructuring costs. Some apparel and footwear businesses reduced inventories and right-sized operations. The page also introduces revenue and pre-tax earnings summaries for Service, Retailing, Pilot, and McLane.

nodes.title: Pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues
Service
nodes.summary: The text reports segment financial results and discusses service and retailing businesses. Service includes aviation services, TTI electronics distribution, restaurant franchising, equipment and furniture leasing, logistics, media, construction management and broadcasting; McLane is reported separately. In 2024, service revenue rose slightly to $20.7 billion, while pre-tax earnings fell 23% and margins declined, mainly due to TTI, aviation services and XTRA. It explains 2024 revenue and earnings drivers, including aviation and IPS growth, TTI’s inventory-related sales decline, and higher aviation costs. For 2023, service revenue rose 8.3%, partly from IPS and aviation, while pre-tax earnings fell 1.7%; TTI weakened and aviation improved. Retailing includes BHA auto dealerships, home-furnishings businesses and other specialty retailers; Pilot is reported separately. Retail revenue fell 1.2% in 2024, with BHA and Louis exceptions, as home furnishings and other retailers faced lower sales, competition and sluggish demand.

nodes.title: Retailing
nodes.summary: The text reviews service, retailing and Pilot performance. In 2024, service revenues and earnings fell amid excess inventories, price competition, fewer XTRA leases, and higher aviation and operating costs; it also compares 2023 with 2022, including IPS acquisition effects and aviation growth. It describes retail businesses and their revenue and earnings trends for 2024 and 2023, including automotive, home furnishings and other retailers. Finally, it explains Pilot’s operations, ownership changes and consolidation dates, and gives its revenue, costs, interest and pretax earnings for 2024 and 2023 periods.

nodes.title: Pilot Travel Centers
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2024 and 2023 operating results for retailing, Pilot Travel Centers, McLane and non-controlled businesses. Retailing earnings fell in 2024 due to weaker vehicle margins and other retailers’ lower sales/margins; 2023 revenue was nearly flat and earnings unchanged, with BHA gains offset by declines elsewhere. Pilot’s ownership and consolidation history, financial results and 2024 revenue and earnings declines are detailed, including margin, expense and borrowing changes. McLane’s business mix, customer concentration and 2024–2023 revenue and earnings trends are summarized. Non-controlled earnings declined in 2024 and rose in 2023, mainly reflecting Kraft Heinz, Occidental and Pilot results and the change in Pilot accounting.

nodes.title: McLane
nodes.summary: Pilot’s 2024 revenue fell 17.4% ($9.9 billion), mainly from lower fuel prices and non-core fuel volumes; pre-tax earnings fell 41.9% as lower diesel margins and higher operating costs outweighed reduced interest expense. Pilot refinanced third-party debt with a $5.7 billion affiliate loan in March, repaying $1.0 billion during 2024; affiliate interest is reported as insurance investment income. McLane wholesales grocery, consumer and beverage products; retail and restaurant sales are high-volume, low-margin and concentrated among significant customers. In 2024, revenue declined 1.3% as restaurant sales fell 5.7% amid lower dining unit volumes while retail sales rose 1.0%; earnings increased 39.3% due to improved gross margins despite lower sales and higher expenses. In 2023, revenue declined 1.1% to $52.6 billion, with lower retail and restaurant sales partly offset by beverage growth; earnings rose 67.9%, supported by slightly higher margins, other income and lower fuel costs, partly offset by personnel expenses.

nodes.title: Non-Controlled Businesses
nodes.summary: Non-controlled business earnings reflect Berkshire’s shares of Kraft Heinz, Occidental, Berkadia and Pilot; they fell $231 million in 2024, mainly from lower Kraft Heinz earnings and Pilot’s absence, after rising $222 million in 2023 due chiefly to Occidental and Kraft Heinz, partly offset by lower Pilot earnings. Berkshire ended equity-method accounting for Pilot after gaining control in January 2023; Kraft Heinz earnings include impairment effects. Investment gains produced net earnings of $41.6 billion in 2024, $58.9 billion in 2023 and a $53.6 billion loss in 2022. These results mainly reflect volatile unrealized equity-price changes, plus gains or losses on securities sold and foreign-exchange effects; 2023 included a $3.0 billion Pilot remeasurement gain. Taxable gains on securities sold varied substantially. Berkshire considers investment gains and losses to have little analytical or predictive value for evaluating periodic performance.

nodes.title: Other
nodes.summary: The text presents after-tax other earnings for 2022–2024, including acquisition accounting expenses, corporate interest expense before currency effects, foreign exchange gains on Berkshire and BHFC debt, and other earnings. Acquisition charges mainly reflect amortization of acquired intangible assets. Currency gains resulted from U.S. dollar strengthening against the euro, pound and yen, which lowered debt’s dollar value; such gains or losses can be significant and volatile. Other earnings mainly comprise parent investment income, intercompany interest income, corporate expenses and unallocated taxes, and rose $484 million in 2024 and $337 million in 2023, primarily due to higher interest income, including on intercompany loans.

Reviews pre-tax earnings and operating trends across service, retailing, Pilot, McLane and non-controlled businesses, including business activities, revenues, margins, earnings drivers and year-over-year comparisons. Covers Pilot’s ownership, consolidation, financing and results; McLane’s sales mix, customer concentration and performance; non-controlled earnings and investment gains or losses, including their volatility and limited predictive value; and other after-tax earnings, acquisition amortization, corporate interest, foreign-exchange effects and parent investment income.

nodes.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis Financial Condition
nodes.summary: Berkshire reports strong liquidity and capital, with 2024 equity of $649.4 billion and earnings of $89.0 billion, including volatile investment gains. It repurchased $2.9 billion of stock under a program that preserves at least $30 billion in cash and Treasury bills. Year-end liquidity was $318.0 billion; securities totaled $287.0 billion, with substantial equity purchases and sales. The company acquired Pilot’s remaining stake and BHE repurchased shares. The text details $124.8 billion of borrowings and debt activity across Berkshire, BHFC, BNSF and BHE, including 2025 BHE issuance; Berkshire does not guarantee BNSF or BHE debt. Operating cash flow was $30.6 billion after taxes, and capital spending was $19.0 billion, with BNSF and BHE forecasting $14.0 billion for 2025.

It describes how property and casualty unpaid-loss liabilities are estimated for reported and IBNR claims, how claim-tail length and legal factors affect uncertainty, and reports $147.6 billion in claim liabilities, 74% attributable to GEICO and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group.

Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group
nodes.summary: The text explains GEICO and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group (BHRG) methods, assumptions, uncertainty and sensitivity in estimating unpaid property and casualty claims. It reports reserve balances, reinsurance recoverables, case and IBNR liabilities, and 2024 favorable reserve development and earnings effects. It discusses reinsurance data limitations, reporting delays, coverage disputes and audits; actuarial methods and differing approaches for short- and long-tail claims; and the possibility of adverse casualty development, including a five-percent sensitivity estimate.

nodes.title: Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: Retroactive reinsurance covers losses from events predating contract inception, mainly long-tail casualty and liability claims. At year-end 2024, gross unpaid losses were $32.4 billion; remaining payments are expected not to exceed $47 billion, and losses are considered unlikely to reach that cap or vary by more than 15% from estimated gross liabilities. Estimates use contract-level exposure, trends, scenarios, judgment, payment activity and reports, with reassessment when circumstances change. Asbestos and environmental liabilities were $11.9 billion; incomplete claims data, mass torts, and legal or regulatory changes create uncertainty. Deferred charge assets were $8.8 billion and are expected to fall $830 million in 2025, reducing pretax earnings correspondingly. Ultimate liabilities rose $196 million in 2024, mostly for casualty exposures; related deferred-charge changes left underwriting results insignificantly affected.

nodes.title: Other Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2024, the company reported $83.9 billion of goodwill and $18.9 billion of indefinite-lived intangible assets. It tests these assets annually and when impairment indicators arise, estimating fair values using methods such as market data, earnings multiples, and discounted cash flows, with forecasts and discount rates as key inputs. These estimates involve substantial judgment and uncertainty, and actual results may differ. Carrying values above fair value result in impairment charges, subject to a goodwill cap. The company concluded goodwill was not more likely than not impaired, but adverse market, economic, business, or industry developments could lead to future losses.

nodes.title: Other Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: In the 2024 fourth-quarter goodwill impairment review, seven reporting units had estimated fair values less than 20% above carrying values. PCC’s fair value exceeded its $28.5 billion carrying value, including $7.5 billion goodwill, by nearly 20%. Pilot, the largest of three units acquired in late 2022 and early 2023, was valued at about $20.3 billion versus $18.3 billion carrying value, including $6.5 billion goodwill. The other five units had aggregate fair value of $11.7 billion, about 12% above carrying value, which included $4.6 billion goodwill.

Equity Price Risk
nodes.summary: The disclosure describes market risks affecting assets and liabilities, especially equity prices, interest rates, foreign exchange rates, and commodities, and notes investment fair-value volatility. Equity investments are the largest portfolio component, historically concentrated in a few issuers; five companies represented about 71% of equity fair value at year-end 2024. Long holding periods, expected short-term volatility, and capital and liquidity buffers are discussed. A table reports equity-security fair values for 2024 and 2023 and estimated after-tax earnings and fair-value effects of hypothetical 30% price increases or decreases, excluding equity-method Kraft Heinz and Occidental stocks; the scenarios are not worst-case outcomes, and losses could be much greater.

nodes.title: Interest Rate and Foreign Currency Risks
nodes.summary: The page describes interest-rate risk from investments and debt, the use of credit ratings to limit borrowing costs, and the general absence of derivatives or asset-liability maturity matching. It explains how rates and other market factors affect fair values and presents hypothetical 2024 and 2023 sensitivity estimates for significant assets and liabilities, including a preferred-stock note. It also notes foreign-currency exposures from subsidiaries, transactions, and multinational-company investments, with little currency matching or derivative hedging.

nodes.title: Market Risks and Internal Control
nodes.summary: The page reports 2024 and 2023 foreign-currency gains and losses in net earnings and other comprehensive income, and explains exposure through foreign subsidiaries and dollar-denominated assets and liabilities. Commodity risks arise from subsidiary operations and are generally managed through customer pricing, with limited use of derivatives; failure to pass on cost increases may hurt results. It refers readers to Item 7’s market-risk disclosures. Management evaluated internal controls under the COSO 2013 framework and concluded they were effective at December 31, 2024; Deloitte audited their effectiveness.

It presents historical fair values, currency gains and losses, and hypothetical market sensitivities, noting scenarios are not worst cases and risks may be greater. It also describes commodity-cost pass-through risks, refers to Item 7 disclosures, and reports effective internal controls under the COSO 2013 framework, audited by Deloitte.

key_items: Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The auditors report on their audits of Berkshire Hathaway’s 2024 and 2023 balance sheets, three years of financial statements, and 2024 internal controls. They conclude the statements fairly present the company’s financial position, results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP, and that internal controls were effective. Management’s responsibilities and the auditors’ independence, PCAOB standards, audit objectives, risk-based procedures, testing, evaluations, and basis for reasonable assurance are described.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Internal control over financial reporting is designed to provide reasonable assurance that external financial statements comply with generally accepted accounting principles. It includes policies and procedures for accurate records of transactions and asset dispositions, authorized recording of transactions and receipts and expenditures, and prevention or timely detection of unauthorized asset use that could materially affect financial statements. Such controls may not prevent or detect misstatements, and future effectiveness may decline due to changing conditions or reduced compliance.

How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The text describes two critical audit matters: estimates of ordinary and retroactive-reinsurance unpaid losses and loss adjustment expenses, whose subjective assumptions required significant auditor judgment and actuarial specialists.
