nodes.title: Accounting Policies, Consolidation, and Estimates
key_items: (a) Nature of operations and basis of consolidation
(b) Use of estimates in preparation of financial statements
nodes.summary: Berkshire is a diversified holding company; its statements consolidate controlled subsidiaries and qualifying variable-interest entities, eliminate intercompany balances, and separately present railroad, utilities, and energy businesses. 2023 Pilot balances were reclassified for comparison with 2024, without changing reported totals or results. GAAP financial statements rely on estimates, especially for insurance claims, reinsurance, fair values, impairments, and credit losses; economic, geopolitical, industry, or company changes may require future adjustments, and actual results may differ.

nodes.title: (c) Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments in U.S. Treasury Bills
nodes.summary: Cash equivalents include demand deposits, money market accounts, and investments with purchase maturities of three months or less; Treasury bill investments mature in over three months but under one year. Fixed-maturity securities are classified as held-to-maturity, trading, or available-for-sale; the company holds available-for-sale securities at fair value, amortizes premiums or discounts using the interest method, and recognizes sale gains and losses, credit losses in earnings, and noncredit unrealized losses in other comprehensive income. Equity securities are at fair value, with changes in earnings. Equity-method investments reflect significant influence (generally over 20% voting interest), proportionate earnings, losses and comprehensive income, contributions and distributions; loss recognition may continue when carrying value reaches zero if other investments are at risk. Loans, mainly manufactured-home loans, are generally held at amortized cost less expected-credit-loss allowances; fees, costs, premiums and discounts adjust yield over loan lives. Loss estimates incorporate noncollection risk, loan performance, historical and collateral data, modified-loan cash flows, current conditions, and forecasts.

nodes.title: Accounting for Investment Securities
nodes.summary: Fixed-maturity securities are classified as held-to-maturity, trading, or available-for-sale; the company holds them as available-for-sale, amortizes premiums or discounts using the interest method, and recognizes gains, losses, and credit impairment in earnings or other comprehensive income as appropriate. Equity securities are measured at fair value, with changes in earnings. The equity method applies to significant-influence investments, generally presumed above 20% voting interest, subject to exceptions; carrying values reflect the investor’s share of earnings, losses, and comprehensive income, cost of additions, and distributions, with possible recognition of further losses when the investment reaches zero.

nodes.title: (g) Loans and finance receivables
nodes.summary: Loans and finance receivables are mainly manufactured-home loans, carried at amortized cost with expected-credit-loss allowances; fees, costs, premiums, and discounts adjust yield over loan terms. Loss estimates consider performance, historical and forecast factors, collateral, and modified cash flows. Loans become delinquent after 30 days, nonaccrual after 90 days, and non-performing upon foreclosure; policies cover interest recognition, collections, charge-offs, and modifications. Other receivables, including reinsurance recoverables, are stated net of allowances, with losses estimated using history, forecasts, counterparty credit, offsets, and enhancements; balances are charged off after collection efforts. Derivatives are recorded at fair value, net of permitted offsets, with changes recognized in earnings or regulated balances. Fair value reflects orderly market-participant transactions, accounting for illiquidity, valuation judgment, and liability credit risk. Inventories include products, supplies, and homes for sale; most use FIFO or average cost, while 32% used LIFO at year-end 2024, with non-LIFO inventory at lower of cost or net realizable value and LIFO replacement-cost excess disclosed.

nodes.title: Receivables, Derivatives, and Fair Value Policies
nodes.summary: Describes receivables’ scope, short-term nature, expected-credit-loss estimates, reinsurance credit reviews, and charge-offs; derivative fair-value balance-sheet presentation, netting, and recognition of valuation changes in earnings or regulated utility accounts; and fair-value principles, market assumptions, valuation adjustments for illiquid or disorderly markets, liability credit risk, and estimation uncertainty.

nodes.title: (k) Inventories
nodes.summary: Inventories include manufactured goods, products acquired for resale, materials and supplies, and homes built for sale. Manufactured inventory cost includes materials, direct and indirect labor, and factory overhead. At December 31, 2024, LIFO valued 32% of consolidated inventories; the remainder was valued primarily using FIFO and average cost. Non-LIFO inventories are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value. Current or replacement costs exceeded LIFO costs by approximately $2.3 billion at December 31, 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: (l) Property, plant and equipment and equipment held for lease
nodes.summary: The policy covers capitalization of property, plant, equipment and leased equipment, including construction costs, interest and regulated-asset financing allowances; routine repairs are expensed. It explains regulator-approved group depreciation for utilities and railroads, retirement and disposal gain/loss treatment, depreciation methods and useful-life ranges across business types, and impairment reviews triggered by adverse changes or held-for-sale status. Impairments are measured against recoverable amounts and recorded at fair value, with regulatory effects considered for regulated utility and energy assets.

nodes.title: (m) Leases
nodes.summary: The company leases property from others and recognizes right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for its rights to use assets and obligations to pay. Lease payments include fixed amounts and index- or rate-based variable amounts; the lease term is the non-cancellable period. Renewal options are included only when exercise is reasonably certain. Liabilities are generally measured using incremental borrowing rates, and right-of-use assets are reviewed for impairment. For some leases, lease and non-lease components are not separated, and leases of one year or less are not recognized on the balance sheet.

nodes.title: (n) Goodwill and other intangible assets
nodes.summary: Goodwill is the excess of a business’s purchase price over the acquisition-date value of its identifiable net assets. It is tested for impairment at least annually by comparing a reporting unit’s carrying value with fair value, estimated using market data, asset and liability values, or valuation methods such as discounted cash flows and earnings multiples; any excess, capped at goodwill, is expensed. Indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually and when impairment indicators arise, with carrying value above fair value expensed. Fair-value assessments require significant judgment. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized based on benefit consumption or straight-line over useful lives and reviewed for impairment when indicators suggest their carrying amounts may not be recoverable.

nodes.title: (o) Revenue recognition
nodes.summary: Insurance premiums are recognized over coverage periods, at inception for retroactive reinsurance and prepaid annuities, or when due for life reinsurance and periodic annuities; amounts are net of ceded premiums, with experience-rated premiums reflecting estimated losses. Product and service revenue is recognized as control transfers, using standalone prices for multiple obligations and adjusting sales for returns, discounts, penalties, incentives, and applicable taxes; product control generally transfers at pickup, delivery, or acceptance, while qualifying custom manufacturing contracts recognize revenue over time. Freight revenue is recognized as transport services are performed, net of shipment-based incentives. Regulated utility and energy revenue is recognized as energy or services are delivered, including billed and unbilled amounts, with estimated refunds accrued where rates are provisional. Other services are recognized over time or upon completion, and leasing revenue ratably or based on usage, mainly under operating leases.

nodes.title: (p) Losses and loss adjustment expenses
nodes.summary: The text describes how liabilities for unpaid property and casualty losses and adjustment expenses are recognized for events occurring by the balance sheet date, measured as undiscounted estimated ultimate payments. Estimates use policyholder and cedent reports, individual case estimates, and incurred-but-not-reported losses. Earnings expenses include paid claims, settlement costs, and changes in estimated liabilities, net of reinsurance recoveries and estimated recoverables. Ceding companies remain responsible to policyholders despite reinsurance.

nodes.title: (q) Retroactive reinsurance contracts
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting policies for retroactive reinsurance, including loss liabilities and deferred charge assets adjusted for updated payment estimates; insurance acquisition costs, their capitalization and amortization for short- and long-duration contracts; life, annuity and health benefit liabilities, cash-flow assumptions, annual reviews, discount-rate updates and related earnings or OCI effects; regulated utility regulatory assets and liabilities, their amortization and reassessment; and foreign-currency translation and transaction gains or losses.

nodes.title: Insurance and Regulated Business Accounting Policies
key_items: (s) Life, annuity and health insurance benefits
nodes.summary: The page explains how successful insurance acquisition costs are capitalized, recoverability-tested, and expensed over contract terms, while other underwriting costs are expensed as incurred. It describes measurement of long-duration life, annuity, and health benefit liabilities using expected cash flows, net premiums, mortality, morbidity, lapse, and discount-rate assumptions; assumptions are reviewed annually, with changes reflected in earnings or other comprehensive income. Regulated utilities defer qualifying costs and revenues as regulatory assets and liabilities, amortize them over future periods, and assess whether recovery or return through rates remains probable.

nodes.title: (u) Foreign currency
nodes.summary: Foreign-currency financial statements are translated using average rates for revenues and expenses and period-end rates for assets and liabilities, with translation effects in accumulated other comprehensive income; transaction and remeasurement gains or losses enter earnings. Income tax policies cover consolidated and jurisdictional filings, current and deferred taxes, tax-rate changes, valuation allowances, and uncertain positions, including related interest and penalties. In 2024, Berkshire adopted tax-credit investment and segment-disclosure standards. Future standards address income-tax disclosures and expense disaggregation. SEC climate-disclosure rules were stayed pending judicial review.

nodes.title: Income Taxes and 2024 Accounting Pronouncements
nodes.summary: Berkshire files consolidated U.S. federal returns with eligible subsidiaries and also files state, local, and foreign returns. Current taxes reflect expected taxable income and expenses; deferred taxes arise from book-tax basis differences, with other-comprehensive-income items recorded there, tax-rate changes recognized upon enactment, and valuation allowances used when asset realization is unlikely. Liabilities, including related interest and penalties, are recorded for uncertain tax positions that fail the more-likely-than-not standard. In 2024, Berkshire adopted ASU 2023-02 for eligible affordable-housing tax-credit investments using modified retrospective proportional amortization, recording a $127 million retained-earnings charge. It also adopted ASU 2023-07 retrospectively, requiring significant segment-expense and expanded interim disclosures.

nodes.title: (x) Accounting pronouncements to be adopted subsequent to December 31, 2024

SEC climate-disclosure rules address severe weather, natural conditions, and material climate risks; although initially effective for large accelerated filers beginning in 2025, implementation was stayed pending judicial review.

nodes.title: (27) Contingencies and commitments
nodes.summary: The note covers routine litigation, PacifiCorp wildfire claims, HomeServices antitrust litigation, other legal matters and future commitments. PacifiCorp faces extensive claims from the 2020 and 2022 wildfires, including a U.S. government demand exceeding $900 million, Oregon class-action verdicts and appeals, mass complaints, and further trials. By year-end 2024, it had accrued $2.75 billion in probable losses, recorded $530 million of insurance recoveries, paid $1.2 billion, and had $1.54 billion unpaid; significant additional losses are possible but not estimable. HomeServices settled the Burnett antitrust class action for $250 million, subject to appeal, amid other cases and asserted Texas damages of about $9 billion. NICO accrued a net $490 million charge for a bankruptcy settlement subject to court approval. Other litigation is not expected to be material. Future purchase commitments total $58 billion, including $12 billion in 2025 and $28 billion thereafter.

title: INSIDER TRADING POLICIES AND PROCEDURES

nodes.title: INSIDER TRADING POLICIES AND PROCEDURES (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway’s insider-trading policies explain that securities laws prohibit anyone holding material nonpublic information from trading on it or tipping others, covering Berkshire and other companies’ securities, including potential investments or transactions. Violations can bring civil and criminal penalties, while supervisors may face liability for failing to prevent misconduct. Berkshire cooperates with regulators’ requests to identify employees with relevant information. These policies apply to designated Covered Persons and family members; violations may lead to discipline, including dismissal, regardless of legal penalties.

nodes.title: Definitions of Certain Terms
nodes.summary: Defines key terms in Berkshire Hathaway’s insider-trading policies: the Board, Clearing Officers and their recusal from their own trades, Covered Employees and Persons, Directors, and Family Members. It defines material and nonpublic information, presuming undisclosed Berkshire transactions involving other companies material. Permitted Trading covers approved Rule 10b5-1 plans, specified investment-manager arrangements, and independent discretionary trading designees who have not received relevant material nonpublic information. Trading includes purchases, sales, contracts, gifts, options, derivatives, and other securities transactions.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.summary: Covered Persons may not trade or recommend trading Berkshire securities while possessing material nonpublic Berkshire information, or trade or recommend trading other companies’ securities using material nonpublic information learned through their covered role or qualifying family connection. This includes companies Berkshire has invested in, is considering investing in, has significant transactions with, or accesses information about through investments, commercial relationships, or board service. Unauthorized disclosure of such information is also prohibited; both trading and tipping can lead to civil and criminal charges. The text cites Rajat Gupta’s prison sentence, $13.9 million penalty, and ban from public-company leadership for disclosing confidential Berkshire investment information.

nodes.title: Procedures
key_items: Insider Trading Policies and Procedures Page 4 of 5
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s procedures may be changed or supplemented with additional trading restrictions. Directors and executive officers and their families generally need pre-clearance for Berkshire trades; other covered employees and families may trade without it during the 45 days after annual or quarterly SEC filings if they lack material nonpublic information, but otherwise need pre-clearance. Restrictions also govern Other Company securities when Berkshire is considering or has disclosed an investment position or material transaction: trading may be prohibited before disclosure and require pre-clearance afterward until Berkshire publicly exits, completes, abandons, or ceases considering the matter. Permitted Trading is excepted. Attachment 1 lists publicly disclosed holdings and may be updated; covered persons must certify compliance quarterly using an updateable Attachment 2. Pre-clearance does not remove personal legal duties, and approved trades must occur within five business days unless otherwise approved. Directors and covered employees should return signed certifications and may consult Berkshire’s CFO.

title: POLICY RELATING TO RECOVERY OF ERRONEOUSLY AWARDED COMPENSATION
summary: The policy requires executive officers to repay or forfeit, as permitted by law and as directed by the Board, awards received on or after December 1, 2023 when they were based on financial results later restated for material securities-law reporting noncompliance, the officer received excess incentive compensation during the preceding three years, and the Board finds recovery in the Company’s and shareholders’ best interests. Independent directors have final, binding authority over applicability and recovery amounts. Award documents incorporate the policy, and recovery supplements other legal or equitable remedies. Adopted December 1, 2023.
